speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To achieve this, the legislation governing charities and charitable fundraising in Singapore should provide a regulatory framework that fosters a safe giving environment, where there is a high level of public trust and confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Yet, our framework must be balanced so as not to stifle charitable work.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Since the Act was last amended in 2010, the charity landscape has continued to evolve and develop.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have therefore reviewed the Charities Act to ensure that our regulatory regime remains relevant and effective to support our vision.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As part of the review, the Commissioner consulted charities across the various sectors, stakeholders, such as the Charity Council and our Sector Administrators, as well as the public on the proposed amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Dialogue sessions were held with charity representatives to explain the rationale for the amendments and understand their concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are heartened by the interest shown in our proposals and the general support given for them.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill before the House today is the outcome of our review and consultation.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Allow me to elaborate on the proposed key amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Together with the key officers and employees, they have a duty to ensure proper management and administration of a charity, including the proper use of charitable assets.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our regulatory regime should therefore ensure that charities are managed by fit and proper persons who can help maintain public trust and confidence in the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The current Charities Act already provides specific grounds to disqualify unfit persons from holding key positions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, a person who has been convicted of an offence involving dishonesty would be disqualified from being a trustee, governing board member or key officer of a charity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Act also specifies the circumstances under which the Commissioner can remove a person from his position in a charity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill seeks to update and strengthen the disqualification and removal regimes in the Charities Act.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, two new grounds for disqualification will be introduced.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Presently, after the conclusion of an inquiry, the Commissioner can, with the consent of the Attorney-General, remove trustees, governing board members, officers, agents or employees of charities from the exercise of their office or employment on the ground of any misconduct or mismanagement of a charity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Next, in this climate of concern about terrorism, the Commissioner is stepping up efforts to counter money laundering and terrorism financing in order to better protect the integrity of the charity sector and its stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The next amendment expands the list of capacities in which disqualified persons cannot act.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is to ensure that the disqualified person will not participate in key decision-making fora of a charity through another entity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Given this proposed amendment, section 28 of the Act is also proposed to be amended to clarify that it is an offence for a person to act in any capacity from which he is disqualified.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The amended section 28 further makes it an offence to contravene an order by the Commissioner to repay moneys received while acting in a disqualified capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Allow me to move on to the proposals relating to the removal regime.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, section 25 will be amended to introduce a new ground for removal, such that the Commissioner can now remove a disqualified person who continues to act as a governing board member or key officer of a charity despite the disqualification.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This enables the Commissioner to intervene should a disqualified person refuse to resign from his position in the charity following the disqualification.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, we propose to allow the Commissioner to declare a person as someone whom the Commissioner would have removed from his position in a charity, if the person resigns before the Commissioner can order his removal.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Currently, before the Commissioner removes a person, for example, on the ground of mismanagement, the Commissioner will first give the person at least one month's notice and an opportunity to make representations.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Should the person resign during this notice period, under the existing provisions, he can no longer be removed by the Commissioner even if there are sufficient grounds to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Subsequently, he would be able to return to a key position in that or any other charity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With the proposed amendment, we will enable the Commissioner to, by an order, declare a person as someone whom the Commissioner would have removed if the person resigns from the charity before the Commissioner can order his removal.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will better safeguard charities and ensure that they are managed by fit and proper persons.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While we seek to strengthen the disqualification and removal regimes, we also recognise the spirit of the Yellow Ribbon Project that encourages the rehabilitation of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Similarly, going forward, it is proposed that the Commissioner will not be able to initiate a removal of a person from his position on the basis of a spent conviction or an offence for which he has been pardoned.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, disqualification will stop once the ground for disqualification ceases.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A person convicted of an offence involving dishonesty will cease to be disqualified when his conviction is spent.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Likewise, a person who was disqualified because he was an undischarged bankrupt will no longer be disqualified once he is discharged from bankruptcy.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, an employee of a charity who was removed by the Commissioner because he was found responsible for mismanagement of the charity's assets would be permanently barred from returning to that charity as an employee, and from holding key positions in any charity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Taking another example, should a board member of a charity with frequent interactions with youth be convicted of having sex with a minor and is subsequently removed by the Commissioner, he would be permanently barred from returning to that charity as a board member or a key officer.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This remains the case even if the person's conviction later becomes spent.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is because the reason for the removal does not cease to be a concern even after the conviction becomes spent.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The person can still serve or be employed in the charity sector in other capacities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Charities Act, with the proposed amendments, will provide a strong yet reasonable regulatory framework, one that seeks to ensure that our charities are managed by persons of integrity and that the interests and good reputation of our charities are protected.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It should also provide effective means to address any abuse.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is to safeguard public interest and trust, so that the public can continue to support charitable causes with confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Fundraisers are increasingly going online, turning to social media and crowdfunding platforms to garner support for their charitable initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The reach of such online fundraising appeals can be significant, raising substantial amounts of donations.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A recent example reported in the news is the case of a baby who was born with only part of her esophagus and whose parents raised S$1.2 million, largely online, to help her get specialist surgery in the US.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is heartening to see Singaporeans responding generously to these appeals.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: However, the reach and scale of these online appeals highlight the need for a regulatory regime that promotes transparency and accountability so as to maintain a high level of trust and integrity, including in the online giving environment.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, this means that fundraisers are subject to basic regulatory requirements, such as the duty to provide clear and accurate information to donors as well as to manage and use donation moneys responsibly.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, this means that where there is misconduct in any fundraising activity, the Commissioner can act to protect donors, for example, by prohibiting or restricting that activity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have consulted the public and held dialogues with charity representatives on the proposed amendment and have explained our policy position.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Like them, we are mindful of the need to refrain from over-regulation, which could stifle charitable efforts as well as charitable giving.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will review our fundraising regulations to minimise administrative burden on small-scale and private fundraising efforts, in particular, appeals for local causes, and exempt them from some of the requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, we will not expect detailed accounts to be maintained for a small fundraising effort conducted among family and friends for a local cause.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On the other hand, charities and institutions of a public character (IPCs), who count fundraising activity as one of their core functions, will be subject to the regulatory requirements of maintaining proper accounting records and keeping fundraising expenses within the specified limits.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These institutions, which enjoy tax benefits for their charity and IPC status, have a public duty to ensure high standards of accountability and good governance in managing their charitable funds.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In relation to the online giving space, I would like to share with the House that we are co-developing with the major crowdfunding platforms in Singapore an industry Code of Practice.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Code will set out recommended practices for fundraising platforms, so that they can be trusted intermediaries for donors and beneficiaries in fundraising for charitable, benevolent and philanthropic purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These submissions are published online for public access.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The proposed amendments to section 48 will formalise this current practice by allowing regulations to be made to mandate the electronic filing of annual submissions and applications.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is part of our efforts to enhance transparency by making information on more charities available online.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we make this change, we will support the charities in electronic filing.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Charities can tap on our voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs)-Charities Capability Fund to purchase computers.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are also working with partners to set up shared services to support smaller charities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill also introduces and amends various provisions to promote compliance with our regulatory requirements and ensure consistency in the penalties prescribed.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Section 18 of the Act is proposed to be amended to make it an offence if a charity, without reasonable cause, fails to preserve accounting records, financial statements and annual reports for five years.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill also clarifies that there does not have to be a persistent default before an offence is committed under section 18.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Currently, contravention of some of the IPC regulations result in a penalty that is lighter than that incurred by non-IPC charities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill proposes to amend section 40C of the Act to allow consistency, across both IPC and non-IPC charities, in the penalty for contravention of regulations, other than for wrongful issuance of tax deduction receipts.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For that, the existing financial penalty will be retained.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill also proposes amendments to align the penalties for serious offences under the Act.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, the penalties for a person acting whilst disqualified and for supplying false or misleading information to the Commissioner have been increased to meet the current levels of penalties prescribed for other offences of similar severity, such as for falsely holding out as a registered charity or IPC.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Next, on enhancing regulatory powers of the Commissioner to safeguard public trust and confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Allow me to move on to the next set of amendments that seek to enhance the regulatory powers of the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At present, after an inquiry against a charity has been instituted and that the Commissioner is satisfied that there is a need to protect the charity, he may, with the consent of the Attorney-General, suspend a person from the exercise of his office or employment with the charity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: However, the suspension is for a maximum of 12 months and this has proven to be insufficient in some cases.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, in complex cases where investigations into financial transactions over an extended period of time are required, the inquiry may take more than a year to complete.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Next, the Bill seeks to enable more timely intervention by the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Section 39B of the current Act allows the Commissioner to prohibit or restrict a fundraising appeal in certain circumstances, such as when the appeal is found to be improperly administered.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: However, such prohibition and restriction orders can only be issued after the completion of investigations.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As investigations may take some time, the donating public may be exposed to questionable fundraising activities in the interim.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This can be done if the Commissioner has reason to suspect, for example, that the appeal is not being properly conducted.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill also proposes to make it an offence if the suspension order is contravened.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The suspension order is akin to a Stop Work Order while investigations are ongoing, and can be followed up with a prohibition or restriction order if irregularities are indeed found.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This would facilitate the Commissioner's work, such as when conducting ongoing monitoring of a charity under investigation, as there will not be a need to raise a new order each time new documents or information become available.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Charities play an important role in our society by meeting the needs of underserved communities, providing essential services and championing causes close to our hearts.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They are instrumental in building a caring and cohesive society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is only with strong public support that the sector can thrive and continue to benefit our community.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Reputation is key to the sector, and one bad apple can erode public trust and confidence in the whole sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The amendments that we are making to the Act, are therefore part of our efforts in ensuring a charity sector that continues to enjoy the trust and support of the community.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are committed to striking the right balance in maintaining a sound and effective regulatory regime that ensures trust and yet, facilitates the good work carried out by the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The enhanced powers of the Commissioner that are proposed by the Bill will not affect the vast majority of charities and fundraisers.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These powers will only be used as a last resort or when there is an urgency to act for the protection of charities and donors.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments underscore the importance of upholding the integrity of charities, inter alia, management, reporting and fundraising.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding, I seek a few clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Whilst I support the amendment to section 16, I seek clarification as to why subsections 2 and 3 are sought to be amended to apply to "a registered charity or an exempt charity", as opposed to the other sections, such as sections 12 and 13, which simply apply to "charity".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to section 25A, in respect of which I note there is no proposal for amendment, can the Minister clarify the basis for the subsection, which provides that it does not apply to an exempt charity?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The application of subsection 5 results in an anomaly in which a key officer who has been removed as such from a registered charity may also be removed as a member of the charity, but a key officer who has been removed as such from an exempt charity may remain as a member of the charity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Considering that exempt charities are universities, educational institutions, hospitals or religious bodies and so on, we would expect that exempt charities be held to equal, if not more stringent requirements.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The socioeconomic landscape of Singapore today is beyond what our parents and grandparents envisaged when Singapore became independent, and the future landscape will be beyond what our current charity models can hold.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: A rapidly greying population, additional touchpoints and enhanced medical expertise in early intervention, diagnosis and treatment, lifestyle challenges, increased stress points in familial and communal relationships, greater financial uncertainties – there will be an increasing number of people requiring support with more complex needs and more interwoven issues.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The demands will be real and, in some cases, loud.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The challenges facing us today are daunting: more clients to be served, more complex needs, more complex issues, more compliance requirements, higher public expectations, higher operating costs, limited revenue, limited technology capabilities, limited manpower and limited funds.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In four simple words: more needs, less resources.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I surmise that our future challenges would, in essence, be similar but accentuated and, possibly, with a different complexion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to change our charity models before it is too late.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Whilst I do not have the solution, I have a few suggestions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: First and foremost, we need to professionalise the sector.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Although the role of volunteers remains integral to the social service sector, the Singaporean society has developed beyond the early days when charities could be run solely by volunteers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The journey of "professionalisation" will be different for every organisation but it must, in every case, begin and it must never end.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Competent, compassionate and committed professionals are key to the welfare of our clients.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is easy to relate this statement immediately to the frontline professionals providing direct services to the clients, such as therapists, social workers, counsellors, teachers, job coaches, medical and allied health workers, and so on.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The truth is, behind them are quiet troops working to ensure that the organisation functions efficiently, meets compliance requirements and governance standards.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Quiet troops cleaning the premises, raising funds, conducting public education, engaging community partners and supporting the frontline professionals.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Our back-end supporters, they are a critical part of the team, without whom services to our clients will suffer to the ultimate detriment of our clients.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is in the interests of our clients that we attract, retain and develop our professionals and our employees.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: To do so, we must treat them fairly, and I refer specifically to remuneration.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is an issue also recognised by the Government and the National Council of Social Services (NCSS).

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But this is a difficult issue for some members of the public.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Those who work in the charity sector, they too have families, they too have aspirations to provide for their families.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not reasonable or fair to expect those who serve in the charities sector to take a pay cut relative to their peers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: To the public, I request that before we next argue that every cent of all donations must go to the beneficiaries, take a look at our own little child, and ask if Mommy or Daddy should take a pay cut for no reason other than that Mommy or Daddy works in the charities sector.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need good people in the sector and we need to pay them well.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They are the ones who started our charities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They bring with them passion, compassion and skills to the organisation that they serve.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Let us be innovative and creative in the way we work with our volunteers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They can supplement our manpower without an increase in our Expenditure on Manpower (EOM).

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They can provide expertise outside that of our organisation's own professionals.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Give volunteers opportunities to contribute meaningfully, give them a sense of pride as they serve.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, almost half of all charities are small charities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Setting up charities, however small, must continue to be encouraged.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is a good reflection of a healthy, spontaneously caring society, one that is willing to give.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: A small charity is cosy, warm, agile and more responsive to the needs of its clients.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Understandably, however, small charities may have limited resources.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at the numbers, I cannot help but wonder if we could collaborate and what greater impact could be achieved if we collaborated for the benefit of their clients.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Collaboration requires us to be vulnerable, for we share our strengths with others.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But it will strengthen us as a whole.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Collaborate we must, for our clients and, indeed, for the sake of our own organisation.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Let us work together towards cohesion in the midst of our diversity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They and their loved ones have put their well-being in our hands.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They trust us to make the change for them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There is pride and dignity in their work.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We insult them if we expect less of them than we do non-charity employers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They deserve challenges, opportunities and support to grow, to flourish, to accomplish and to serve.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They are walking the journey with our clients and us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Imposing high standards on ourselves is our way of showing our respect to them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The community and the Government have rallied around those who need support.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We, the charities, should be another pillar of support.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We must not continue to be a sector dependent on support.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my fifth point: the sustainability of VWOs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to emphasise that this point is limited to the context of VWOs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: By a conventional approach, we continue to look within ourselves to streamline work processes, better deploy our personnel, increase productivity and, hopefully, reduce reliance on donations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This conventional approach, while necessary, is not sufficient to see us into the future.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: A very small proportion of the revenue is derived from very low fees or very low revenue from sheltered enterprises, and most sheltered enterprises are loss-making.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The increase in Government funding and donations over the years cannot and will not be able to match the growing rate of needs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Think on this – even the best managed organisation can potentially fall into unsustainable deficit.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we fall into an unsustainable deficit, only two things can happen: a bailout because we cannot afford to fail; and that would entail funds from the public, more likely through Government rescue, or a shutdown resulting in a displacement of clients, loss of employment and disruption in the sector.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: How much of a risk can we stomach?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Whilst Government funding and donations remain desirable, they should no longer be relied upon to form a significant portion of our receipts.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have a vision of a VWO that is firmly rooted to its vision, committed to serve all clients, regardless of status and wealth but it also engages in revenue generation with revenue generated being used to execute our mission and our vision.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Not a new concept, but it is using fees from those who can afford to subsidise fees of those who cannot.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The means testing criteria and methodology is updated to align with this key model, leveraging on its competencies.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It goes regional, it exercises prudence in undertaking appropriate risk management assessment, takes actions to hedge against reasonably anticipated risks.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: All throughout, it remains true to its commitment to serve its clients.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is my vision for a future VWO.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we succeed, we reduce our reliance on public funds.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we fail, we go back to reliance on public funds.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But we need the support and understanding of the public that profits are generated for charitable purposes.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need the support of the Government not to remove our IPC status or compromise our charitable status on that count.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I trust we can work out a feasible model with sufficient safeguards and sufficient latitude for enterprise.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Such a model could be seeded by donations or social impact bonds.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is new to us but we can work on that.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But it is not a model that must be sustained only by donations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we do not operate more profits, we are doomed to fail.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am arguing, submitting for the need to build a model that is financially sustainable to take us into the future.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is difficult for us to live with little.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Compound that difficulty with little or no education, a disability or more, illnesses, failing marriages, single parenthood, difficult children, ailing parents, estranged relations, difficult employment situations and difficult community situations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Is it surprising that many of us spiral downwards, physically, emotionally, spiritually and financially?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government and the charities, rightly, must step in to help.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The support must be relevant, effective and empowering.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Such intervention and support can, at best, only solve an immediate problem.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We must, in the long run, empower and encourage our people to take ownership of their lives so that they can break out of the vicious charity cycle and, in turn, reach out to support others.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of scurrying for additional resources to support an increasing number of people, we build a strong network within this community to support each other, more than what money can buy.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: From a relational perspective, "charity" or "welfare" connotes the dispensation of help from one to the other.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It creates a difference in status and widens the social gap.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It accentuates the chasm in mobility, socially, physically, economically and politically.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is liable to create a sense of low self-worth and helplessness in the other party.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: What we call ourselves shape what we think of ourselves and shapes our aspirations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some are mismanaged and fail to deliver what they promised to their clients and their donors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How would you define a charity as a good one?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Good governance and management, competence and transparency in the way it handles its operations and in the way it disburses its funds to its clients and serves the community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore welcome and support the amendments to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I have a few clarifications which I hope the Minister could clarify.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Charities generally work for the good of the society, and they work together with State institutions to ensure that funds are channelled to the right cause or beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Without charities − good charities − our society would be poorer.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As Singapore and Singaporeans become more affluent, the culture of paying it forward and giving back to society is gaining greater traction.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is heartening, therefore, to note that fellow Singaporeans are stepping up to help those who have fallen through the cracks and those who are in dire need.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Media reports of Singaporeans coming forward to help and assist, both in Singapore and overseas, is heartwarming and it could take many different forms.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There was a recent newspaper report of a senior citizen who was sponsored on a trip to Paris simply for him to see the Eiffel Tower by a very generous but anonymous donor.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He came back realising, however, that his own plywood version of the Eiffel Tower that he had spent many months making was, in fact, structurally incorrect.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Amusing though the story may be, it highlights the fact that many Singaporeans are willing to give to different needs and different wants.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They also do not want to be made known that they are the donors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This, in my view, is perhaps the mark of an altruistic donor.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it can also lead to abuse by unscrupulous canvassers of donations and the recipients themselves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps, even worse, the situation may be worse if the person or persons in charge of collecting and disbursing funds is/are caught with their hands in the till!

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As an example, many of us in this House, perhaps, have worked with an organisation called Project Awareness, a social initiative for the needy, and they came under the spotlight about four years ago.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At that time, its project coordinator, an undischarged bankrupt, had his bank number listed as a repository for donations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Rightfully so, the Commissioner of Charities stepped in at the right moment and made sure that Project Awareness set their house in order, and issued an order to stop them from canvassing for funds while they were rectifying their internal structures.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, Project Awareness continues to do good work and has a professional team managing their funds.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I would be grateful if the Minister could share with the House if there have been such cases and how many have come under the Ministry's view?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How much has been collected by these so-called charities?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am asking this because many Singaporeans may have contributed to such charities or initiatives unwittingly, borne out of emotion and parochialism.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Those preying on the naivete of Singaporeans who come forward to share what they have, should be taken to task.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fundraising appeals are evolving as quickly as the social landscape.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I seek clarification on when, which date this will be specifically issued, and how much force it would have under the law to regulate these sites.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By doing so, it will ensure transparency and accountability because much-needed social values when soliciting funds from the public must be upheld.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It will also be made incumbent upon recipients to declare that they are not receiving state funds to alleviate their plight under the new guidelines.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A recipient who is getting crowdfunding support in addition to state support may deprive another more deserving client from obtaining funds.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That is where accountability and verification of facts come in handy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Commissioner of Charities, Dr Ang Hak Seng, had stated very clearly, "If you declared that you did not get Government aid but you did, it is a misrepresentation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You did not tell people the whole picture when you asked for donations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If your need is fake, you bet I will look into the matter." By according the Commissioner of Charities more power, misconduct will and can be prevented, and the people's trust and faith in their fellow Singaporeans will be preserved, and the willingness to share and give more will become more widespread and the Singapore society, in general, will become all the more richer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have some concerns regarding the changes to the definitions and coverage of key officer and fundraising appeal, which are important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned that the onerous liability imposed by the amendments will discourage people who are wanting to serve in charities, especially smaller charities where management resources may be limited, and that, in turn, puts pressure on people wanting to serve.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will the Ministry allay such fears and encourage more volunteers to step up and serve in charities, both big and small?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seems to me that the existing scope of fundraising appeal to members of the public will now be expanded quite considerably, beyond the members of the public.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the explanation note to the Bill, the Ministry cited a new example of an appeal by an unincorporated association to its members.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The existing law applies to an appeal to members of the public and does not cover private appeal or donations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the explanation note in the Bill stops there, without any further elaboration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It does not elaborate adequately on its expanded coverage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, unsolicited donations – the Ministry's comments to public feedback during the public consultation process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry also stated that this can now include unsolicited donations and appeals to grant-making philanthropic organisations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The explanation note to the Bill does not, however, confirm this or say anything about it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unsolicited donations, as its name suggests, are donations made purely voluntarily and without any initiative or action on the part of the charity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is therefore extremely odd to include such donations as part of fundraising appeals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there any particular recent incident which caused the Ministry to think that the expanded coverage is absolutely necessary?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, will the Minister share with the House some of the details of the incident and how they led the Ministry to propose these changes?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My Deputy Speaker, I would also like to know from the Minister what changes the Ministry will be making to the fundraising regulations, which will apply specifically to unsolicited donations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As regards to grant-making philanthropic organisations, may I clarify with the Minister how the amendment affects them and whether we are talking about such organisations making appeals for donations to fund the grants or assistance they render to members of the public?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, private fundraising within schools, associations and religious organisations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it seems that besides grant-making philanthropic organisations, the coverage will be extended to other non-charity fundraisers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministries said that it is important for the Commissioner to be able to stop improper fundraising.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I am concerned that this may also discourage many sincere and well-meaning Singaporeans in their different organisations from raising funds for very good reasons, not to mention the resulting bureaucratic hooks that will be imposed on non-charity fundraisers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister also clarify whether this new definition of fundraising appeal and the fundraising appeal regulations to be amended will apply to all types of fundraising by schools, associations and religious organisations, or whether it will cover only a certain limited mode of fundraising?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, will it apply to religious organisations raising funds by auctions, for example, as we often see during temple or seventh-month dinners?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry stated in their comments to public feedback during consultation that the Ministry would be reviewing fundraising regulations to make sure that the requirements will not apply to small fundraising efforts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not sure if I heard the Minister correctly in her speech just now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On crowdfunding regime, given the new expanded definition of fundraising appeal, I would also like to ask the Minister to confirm whether the new regulation, the new regime, also applies to online crowdfunding.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it seems that it will not be mandatory.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do hope that however well-meaning this code may be, the code or any intended regulation will not stifle or discourage Singaporeans from continuing their acts of charity through crowdfunding.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On to my conclusion on the fundraising appeal point.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears to me that significant amendments will need to be made to the current subsidiary legislations on fundraising regulations to cover the expanded scope of fundraising appeal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think we should know now, if not later, that sufficient details about what the impending regulatory changes are.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would have preferred that this Bill would have shed more light on these details or the explanatory note in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The House should, in fact, assess this Bill with the changes the Ministry intends to make in the subsidiary legislations to know what is the ultimate package that the public can expect.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My Deputy Speaker, in conclusion, I agree that it is good to encourage good governance among our charities, in our fundraising efforts, for example.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the time, I believe that we should also be mindful that requirements are not too impractical or onerous that they create additional or unnecessary burdens on our charities, their staff and volunteers as well as non-charities and well-meaning Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments will bring about stronger regulation of charities in order to gain better public trust and confidence.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The requirement for accountability would help to ensure that all fundraising activities are subjected to thorough scrutiny and abuses as well as exploitations are avoided.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is there any way to make the usage of the funds more transparent, as the Minister has said it will be regulated, especially for Institutions of Public Character (IPCs)?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can we encourage donations among Singaporeans for a more regulated cause as compared to crowdfunding which is via Internet in an uncontrolled form?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For charitable organisations, is there crowdfunding ethics developed for greater transparencies and improved public trust that the funds raised are put to good use and for the intended purpose?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With reference to clause 8(c) section 25(4)(4A) and clause 9(9) section 28, have there been previous cases or incidents where disqualified persons still remained in key positions and have there been any adverse impact or misuse of donations?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is natural for public to be disappointed and alarmed to hear that such disqualified persons still remain in those key positions or continued to assume key positions in one or more charities without being removed from the position or barred from being in one.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: And I welcome the changes in this Bill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In clause 9 section 27(4A), it is laudable that our society is gradually being receptive, inclusive and embracing ex-offenders by giving them second chances, in support of the Yellow Ribbon Project initiatives.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, will there be any exceptional provision where such persons will be barred or disqualified forever, even if their charges are spent?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There have been some worrying perceptions on the ground about charities acting as a conduit for money laundering and terrorism, and this may be unfounded.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, one should take note so as to not overly mention religious charity groups in its publicity, as opposed to other charity groups.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to seek some clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, I would like seek clarification on the definition of a "fundraising appeal".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the increasing popularity of online donations, are online crowdsourcing appeals that leverage social media or other online platforms considered as fundraising appeals as defined in the Act?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If so, how does the Government regulate such online appeals and ensure that the monies donated do end up helping the intended beneficiaries?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there statistics on how many of such online fundraising campaigns turned out to be misrepresentations or half-truths?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are donors able to get their money back if the cause that they had donated to turned out to be misleading or, worse still, untrue?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the COC consider establishing a whistleblowing channel for the public to report possible suspicious online campaigns on a timely basis?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to touch on the proposed mandatory electronic filing of annual submissions and other regulatory submissions by charities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I understand that most charities are already filing their annual submissions electronically via the Charity Portal, I would like to ask how many charities have yet to embrace e-filing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there any plans to assist these charities in e-filing before the mandate kicks in?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I am concerned about the impact on the charity as a whole, and more importantly, its beneficiaries if the charity is under investigation due to a handful of rouge individuals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under the proposed amendments, the COC would be allowed to suspend any fundraising appeals if there is reason to suspect that the appeal is not conducted properly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Does such a clause target the entire charity, causing the organisation to freeze its operations whilst investigations are ongoing?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Or will the COC be able to isolate the rogue individuals involved in the suspicious fundraising appeal and suspend them from participating in the charity while they are being investigated?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The latter scenario would enable charities to continue to function if there so happens to be a bad apple in the barrel.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In closing, I would like to say that, with the expanding popularity of online fundraising appeals, it is timely for us to review the Charities Act to safeguard the public's trust in the charity sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the recent World Giving Index showed that Singaporeans are caring and generous, the sector will need to be well regulated to ensure that we Singaporeans do not and should not grow disillusioned with giving.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I hope the Ministry would take a firmer stance on what I would call "soft deceptions", that is, efforts to paint misleading pictures of persons or families in distress by charities or social organisations so as to attract more funding.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More often than not, whatever information that is not shared in these appeals are actually the vital information.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Very one-sided stories about the potential recipients are painted.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Potential donors are given the impression that Government agencies and existing help groups are not reaching out to assist such families, which may not be the case.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This should not be taken lightly for a few reasons.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, given the limited amount of resources available, such practices end up diverting the necessary funds and resources from truly needy parties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, deliberately or not, they cast doubt on the work and integrity of our Government help agencies and have the potential to undermine them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When people do not have faith in our national help network, they will hesitate to approach them for help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is clearly undesirable, as any delay could push families in distress into disastrous predicaments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Social service organisations are an important and integral part of our help system but they must be on the same page as the Government agencies doing similar work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must require and enable them to perform the necessary background checks on those they desire to assist.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Very recently, a homeless man in the United Kingdom was hailed as a hero in the aftermath of the Manchester suicide bomb attack and well-wishers raised £52,000 for him on a popular crowdfunding website.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It was later revealed that he was a thief who stole from the victims, and the full amount of donations were to be refunded to the donors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need better coordination, exchange and sharing of information between both Government and non-Government help entities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, what about such sites, especially if they are based overseas?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, we should implement stricter criteria for the use of names and photos in connection with fundraising.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There should be clearer regulations for how identities and photos can be used in appeals and publicity materials.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is common to see charities using photographs of celebrities or even politicians to boost support for their work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, support for a particular event cannot be implied as support for fundraising efforts of a charity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During such crises and power struggles, the operations of the organisation suffers and, expectedly, when things become public, donations will drop.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These organisations serve important functions, benefiting many people through the disbursement of rations, healthcare, free meals, bursaries, milk powder, money and so on.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should have a framework and the resources to help charities experiencing temporary problems to at least continue some of their basic operations so that the people receiving help will not experience any disruptions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There should be time limits imposed on when certain impasse must be resolved, beyond which the Government is allowed to step in.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For better governance, the roles and responsibilities of office bearers or key personnel should be clearly defined so that there are curbs and limits on potential abuses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, I request for greater control over phishing appeals for donations on websites which can be accessed from Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Technology, such as data analytics and tools to detect how long a user's eye dwells upon certain areas of a website, is being used to help websites push certain advertisements, including donation appeals, to social media users.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What measures does the Government have to reduce the abuse of such technologies which may prey on the goodwill of Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of the Charities (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I declare that I sit on the board of two large-sized charities serving in the capacity of a volunteer.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Registered charities are exempted from paying income taxes and property taxes pertaining to properties used for that charity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Out of the registered charities in Singapore, about half or more than 1,000 are religious organisations, such as churches and temples.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One in five, about 18%, support social and welfare causes and others in health, healthcare, education, sports, animal welfare and others.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This $2.7 billion donation pie is larger than the size of the current budget of MSF, which I know is about $2.5 billion.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The importance of the charity sector cannot be understated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of them play a key role in our society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of them partner the Government in providing essential services from education to health to social assistance.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some fill the gaps where public goods are lacking.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The more organised and larger religious groups fill the spiritual needs of the lives of citizens, command influences over their congregations and play a role in religious harmony in a multiracial, multireligious society, such as ours.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are several key trends that I have observed in the Singapore society that calls for higher involvement of and greater attention to the charity landscape.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These key trends include: (a) a rapidly ageing population resulting in higher demands for healthcare and other services, and fears of retirement inadequacy; (b) the breaking down of the traditional assumption by both children and parents that question if family should be the first port of call when needs arise in a family; (c) the rise in non-traditional family make-ups, such as transnational family members, single parents either widowed, divorced or unwed; (d) the rise in mental health issues; (e) rise in technology and the prevalence of social media as a way of life, therefore online appeals and cashless transactions are some examples; (f) higher societal expectations as a result of a better educated and vocal population; and (g) the rise of religiousity, religious fundamentalism and risk of terrorism in a Singapore that is home to at least 10 religions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Out of these societal shifts in Singapore arise new causes and areas of passion for which new charities support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is also a notable rise in the number of large-sized charities with more than $10 million income and a rapid rise of the number of new charities seeking registration, both as charities and as IPCs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Even traditional philanthropists have chosen to register their own charities to tap on public funding and tax-exempt benefits to further their own pet causes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This has given rise to public concern and higher scrutiny by the charity watchdogs and most likely contributed also to the review of the Charities (Amendment) Bill today.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, after studying the provisions in the Bill, I would like to raise four areas for the Ministry to consider.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, an Industry Transformation Map; two, on enforcement; three, on the protection of those who acted in good faith; and fourth, the cost of governance.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In particular, I refer to the COC's aspiration to be a "proactive charity advisory" as stated in its Annual Report.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, more than tweaking the Charities Act, the charity "industry" needs a better landscape study and I think an ITM is in order, much like what the Future Economy committees are doing to keep up with the times.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In developing the ITM, we need a better differentiation of charities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The charities landscape is too diverse to segment the players based on the size of their budgets, which is the current way by which the Charities Act is implemented through the Code of Governance.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Charities should be differentiated and treated, even nurtured, according to the different nature, priority, strengths and pitfalls in the different sectors in the charity landscape.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some charities, such as the step-down community hospitals and special schools, were set up to respond to the call of the Government to meet the needs of target beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Surely, the governance of and support of such healthcare and social charities which are developed to complement Government's efforts should be different from those, say, in the religious sector or charities which are just private endeavours.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A more empathic and nurturing hand and touch ought to be provided to those who are the Government's partners, for example, in healthcare, education and other social challenges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is too limiting to police these partners through stringent codes of governance only.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Efforts ought to be made to help future-proof them and ensure their skills and competencies are updated to survive or even thrive in a society that is affected by technological and other social disruptions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The current code of governance applied to all charities according to the tier in which the size of their budgets fall smacks of, to me, a bit simplistic cookie cutter perspective of charities and does not take into account the impact and contribution of different charities to society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, there ought to be a better differentiation of charities, and more should be done for those who are the Government's partners in service delivery in the social landscape especially.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As a "proactive charity advisory", the aspiration of the COC and its partners should also provide greater clarity and direction on the different sectors in the charity landscape.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There ought to be published mini-blueprints of the state of the union in each sector's landscape, strengths, the concerns, areas of needs and strategies to plug any gaps that the Government has not or will not step in.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Potential charities can then be advised by the COC and its partners or even incentivise to direct and deploy resources to where the needs might be.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I can think of emerging and critical needs, such as home-based healthcare services for the elderly, transnational family challenges, services for adults with disabilities and coordination of overlapping services in elderly support, and other areas of needs that I see are less than met.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I can also think of instances by which the COC and its partners can more effectively advise on areas where there are already duplicate or overlapping services to scale down fundraising appeals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: An ITM for the sector should also support the diversity of income generation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A "proactive charity advisory" should not only look at policing the authenticity of fundraising appeals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Effective charities have long been encouraged to be more self-reliant and diversify their income streams so that they do not become over-reliant on only donation appeals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Where they can, charities should develop and learn to develop relevant services that are needed by their beneficiaries and generate other income streams.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This may come in the form of social enterprises or the trading arms of the charities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, although policing of fundraising appeals is important in order to retain public trust in charities, future reviews of the Charities Act should look at how the COC might support, for example, new developments like social enterprises or other forms of income streams in the charities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is well and good to set up a strict regime of governance for the charities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But it is another altogether to effectively enforce it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not uncommon to hear of suspect fundraisers in public places touting for donations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also not uncommon to sight charities who were already put on, say, restrictive orders by the COC to still carry on its activities per normal.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In one of the shops selling religious artefacts in my constituency at Waterloo Mall, I have had complaints by constituents about a business owner collecting donations for themselves in a box next to legitimate donation boxes for the Community Chest.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on protection of those who acted in good faith.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Charities (Amendment) Bill seeks to strengthen the regulatory framework of the COC and to further empower the Commissioner to bring any "Key Persons" to task; all this to make charities more accountable to the public and to its funders.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill proposes that section 2 of the Charities Act be amended to broaden the definition of "Key Persons" who can be brought to task should things go wrong.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As a result, members of a charity who, I quote, "provides advice to the charity on the control and management of the administration of the charity" are now also made accountable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Both poor and good governance comes with a cost.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Charities with poor governance standards often find themselves paying the ultimate price of not just having their key officers and board members taken to task by the law, but also the potential closure of the charities, impacting the lives of its beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Good governance, on the other hand, does not come free either and, in many cases, paid out of the funders or other donors of the charity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The cost of governance includes internal and external audits, legal advice for both strategic and operational issues, costs to comply with constitutional and statutory requirements, and even risk management analysis, which can take a lot of time and effort, not to mention the time expended by the staff, the management and board members of the charity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the UK, Pilotlight Group helps UK charities and social enterprises thrive by harnessing the skills of business leaders.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The scale that it develops test if the board members are too engaged or too unengaged; if the structures and procedures of the charities are too restrictive or too loose, if trustee skills are too narrow or too generic to be of use, and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The COC may wish to study this simple tool to help getting governance just right, in addition to its "comply or explain" and "yes/no" governance checklist.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Under-governance, on the other hand, puts the charity and its core mission at risk.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is much more to do than to get the governance just right.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope the COC and its partners will consider my suggestion for the development of an ITM and I hope that the next review of the Charities Act will be more transformational, more visionary and reflective of the vibrancy and the high potential charities can value-add to society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I offer, in conclusion, the COC my fullest support and assistance if required and I fully support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened to see that there is constant review of the Charities Act, with the last one just seven years ago, and that we continually seek to strengthen accountability in this sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have the privilege of starting my own charity 17 years ago when I was a little boy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Animal Concerns Research and Education Society (ACRES) has a gone a long way since our birth in 2001 in my bedroom in my parents' house.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I actually never told my parents I used our home address as the first ACRES address but I guess now is a good time to tell them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I can tell you that it is not easy starting and running a charity in Singapore and, in fact, many said I would fail when I first started ACRES.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a charity fully dependent on donations, I am aware of the difficulties local charities face in raising funds to sustain their operations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be a great pity to see a rare few black sheep wreak distrust in the charity sector, hampering the necessary work of more than 2,000 registered charities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fundraising success depends on the goodwill of the public, and goodwill is often very fragile, dependent on the level of trust held by the public that the dollar donated makes a positive impact on the lives of the beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Trust hangs by a thread and, once broken, is terribly difficult to restore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thus, I am encouraged that constant reviews and amendments of the Charities Act help to prevent errant behaviour and ultimately, protect the good work of the vast majority of charities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, parts of the Bill may have the contrary effect of hampering the charity sector due to the lack of clarity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Based on feedback I received and also via Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH), there were questions raised about whether an "appeal" includes unsolicited funds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There were also questions on what "a confined group of persons" mean.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the Minister had provided some examples earlier but how do we define small-scale private fundraising?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And these small-scale private fundraising activities are commonplace in the charity sector, for example, a bake sale at a company event, or a birthday party.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, the law will not extend to these cases as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the Ministry be clear on certain types of fundraising appeals which can be exempted from which provisions in this Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Application permits are an administrative hassle and, unless the application process can be simplified, I fear that this may not bode well for charities which conduct activities abroad, such as humanitarian charities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
